title: Projections
summary: The orthogonal projection of a vector onto a line is a scalar multiple of the direction. Onto a subspace, the coefficient vector solves the normal equations, and the residual is orthogonal to every column.
intuition:
Projecting a vector onto a line is the geometry of a shadow. Given a nonzero direction $u$ and a vector $v$, the projection is the multiple of $u$ that lands closest to $v$. The error $v-\mathrm{proj}_u v$ has to be perpendicular to $u$, and that one condition fixes the scalar: $\mathrm{proj}_u v=(u^\top v/u^\top u)\,u$. The denominator is the squared length of $u$, so $u$ does not need to be a unit vector. If it is, the formula collapses to $(u^\top v)u$.

A subspace with several directions is the same idea with a matrix. Let the columns of $A$ be a basis of the subspace, and let $b$ be the vector being projected. The projection is $A\hat x$ for the coefficient vector $\hat x$ that makes the residual $b-A\hat x$ orthogonal to every column. Orthogonality to the columns is the matrix equation $A^\top(b-A\hat x)=0$, which rearranges to the normal equations $A^\top A\hat x=A^\top b$. Full column rank makes $A^\top A$ invertible, so there is one $\hat x$. The residual is then orthogonal to the whole column space, and $A\hat x$ is the closest point of that subspace to $b$.

The matrix that sends every $b$ to its projection is the projection matrix of the projection-matrix lesson, namely $P=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top$ when the columns are independent. That lesson records the algebraic facts $P^2=P=P^\top$, the eigenvalues $0$ and $1$, and the equality of trace and rank. This lesson stops at the vector you land on and at the residual being orthogonal to the columns. Computing $P$ and multiplying is optional once the normal equations have been solved.

definitions.body: For $u\neq 0$, the orthogonal projection of $v$ onto the span of $u$ is $\mathrm{proj}_u v=(u^\top v/u^\top u)\,u$. The residual $v-\mathrm{proj}_u v$ is orthogonal to $u$.
If the columns of $A$ span the target subspace, the coefficient vector $\hat x$ of the projection of $b$ satisfies $A^\top A\hat x=A^\top b$. The projected vector is $A\hat x$.
The residual is $r=b-A\hat x$. When $\hat x$ solves the normal equations, $A^\top r=0$: the residual is orthogonal to every column of $A$, hence to the whole column space.

formulas.name: Geometric projection
formulas.note: Onto a line. The direction $u$ is nonzero and need not be a unit vector.

formulas.name: Normal equations
formulas.note: Onto the column space of $A$. The residual $b-A\hat x$ is orthogonal to that column space. The matrix form of the same map is in the projection-matrix lesson.

properties: On a line, $\mathrm{proj}_u v=(u^\top v/u^\top u)\,u$. The residual is orthogonal to $u$, and $\|v\|^2=\|\mathrm{proj}_u v\|^2+\|v-\mathrm{proj}_u v\|^2$.
On a subspace with basis the columns of $A$, the coefficients solve $A^\top A\hat x=A^\top b$, and the projection is $A\hat x$.
The residual $r=b-A\hat x$ satisfies $A^\top r=0$. It is orthogonal to every column, not merely to one of them.
If $b$ is already in the column space, the residual is $0$ and $A\hat x=b$. Projection does not move a vector that is already in the subspace.
The matrix of this map is treated in the projection-matrix lesson. The identities $P^2=P=P^\top$ belong there; the vector arithmetic belongs here.

examples.title: Projection onto a line in $\mathbb{R}^2$
examples.prompt: Project $v=(3,1)^\top$ onto the span of $u=(1,2)^\top$. Compute the residual and check that it is orthogonal to $u$.
steps: The two scalars are $u^\top v=3+2=5$ and $u^\top u=1+4=5$. The coefficient is $5/5=1$, so $\mathrm{proj}_u v=1\cdot(1,2)^\top=(1,2)^\top$.
Its dot product with $u$ is $1\cdot 2+2\cdot(-1)=0$. The squared lengths add: $\|v\|^2=10$, $\|\mathrm{proj}_u v\|^2=5$, and $\|r\|^2=4+1=5$.
examples.answer: The projection is $(1,2)^\top$ and the residual is $(2,-1)^\top$, which is orthogonal to $(1,2)^\top$.

examples.title: Normal equations for a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$
examples.prompt: Let the columns of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ span the subspace, and let $b=(1,1,0)^\top$. Solve the normal equations and check that the residual is orthogonal to both columns.
steps: First $A^\top A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $A^\top b=(1,1)^\top$. The system $2\hat x_1+\hat x_2=1$, $\hat x_1+2\hat x_2=1$ has solution $\hat x_1=\hat x_2=\tfrac13$.
The projection is $A\hat x=\bigl(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac23\bigr)^\top$. The residual is $b-A\hat x=\bigl(\tfrac23,\tfrac23,-\tfrac23\bigr)^\top$.

Dot the residual with the first column: $\tfrac23+0-\tfrac23=0$. Dot it with the second: $0+\tfrac23-\tfrac23=0$. So $A^\top r=0$. The same point is what the projection matrix of the projection-matrix lesson returns as $Pb$; the matrix identities are proved there.
examples.answer: $\hat x=\bigl(\tfrac13,\tfrac13\bigr)^\top$ and the projection is $\bigl(\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac23\bigr)^\top$. The residual $\bigl(\tfrac23,\tfrac23,-\tfrac23\bigr)^\top$ is orthogonal to both columns.

traps: Forgetting the denominator $u^\top u$. The formula $(u^\top v)u$ is the projection onto a unit vector only. For $u=(1,2)^\top$ it would return $(5,10)^\top$ instead of $(1,2)^\top$.
Solving $Ax=b$ when $b$ is not in the column space. The right equation is $A^\top A\hat x=A^\top b$. The residual is supposed to be orthogonal to the columns, not necessarily zero.

Checking orthogonality of the residual against one column and stopping. $A^\top r=0$ is one equation per column. Both columns in the plane example have to be checked, or the single product $A^\top r$ computed.
Re-deriving $P^2=P=P^\top$ in place of the residual check. Those matrix facts belong to the projection-matrix lesson. Here the object to compute is $\mathrm{proj}_u v$ or $A\hat x$.
python:
def dot(u, v):
    return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))

u, v = [1, 2], [3, 1]
coeff = dot(u, v) / dot(u, u)
proj = [coeff * t for t in u]
resid = [v[i] - proj[i] for i in range(2)]
assert proj == [1, 2]
assert resid == [2, -1]
assert dot(resid, u) == 0
assert dot(proj, proj) + dot(resid, resid) == dot(v, v)

A = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]]
# A^T A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], A^T b = [1, 1], xhat = [1/3, 1/3]
p = [1 / 3, 1 / 3, 2 / 3]
r = [1 - 1 / 3, 1 - 1 / 3, 0 - 2 / 3]
col1, col2 = [1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1]
assert abs(dot(r, col1)) < 1e-12
assert abs(dot(r, col2)) < 1e-12
assert abs(sum(p) - 4 / 3) < 1e-12
print(1)

questions.stem: The orthogonal projection of a vector $v$ onto the span of a nonzero vector $u$ is
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. The coefficient is the dot product $u^\top v$ divided by the squared length $u^\top u$. Option B inverts the fraction. Option D is correct only when $u$ is a unit vector; for $u=(1,2)^\top$ and $v=(3,1)^\top$ it gives the wrong vector $(5,10)^\top$ instead of $(1,2)^\top$.

questions.stem: The columns of $A$ are linearly independent. The coefficient vector of the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space satisfies
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. Orthogonality of the residual to the columns is $A^\top(b-A\hat x)=0$, which is the normal equation $A^\top A\hat x=A^\top b$. The unknown $\hat x$ lives in the coefficient space, whose dimension is the number of columns, so it is not equal to $b$ in general. The residual is zero only when $b$ is already in the column space.

questions.stem: The residual $r=b-A\hat x$ comes from a solution of the normal equations. Which of the following are true?
options: $r$ is orthogonal to every column of $A$.
$r$ is orthogonal to the column space of $A$.
$r$ is the zero vector for every $b$.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. The normal equations are exactly $A^\top r=0$, which says the residual is orthogonal to every column and therefore to every linear combination of the columns. The residual is zero only when $b$ lies in the column space. A vector outside that subspace has a nonzero residual.

questions.stem: Let $u=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $v=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following are true?
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. Here $u^\top v=5$ and $u^\top u=5$, so the projection equals $u$ itself, namely $(1,2)^\top$. The residual is $(3,1)^\top-(1,2)^\top=(2,-1)^\top$, and $(2)(1)+(-1)(2)=0$. The vector $v$ is not on the line, so the projection is not $v$.
The answer is **5**. The projection is $(1,2)^\top$, and $1^2+2^2=5$. As a check, the residual $(2,-1)^\top$ has squared length $5$, and $5+5=10=\|v\|^2$.
